content: Many preterm infants require respiratory support to maintain optimal oxygenation levels. Both hypoxemia (oxygen levels below the optimal range) and hyperoxemia (oxygen levels above the optimal range) are associated with adverse clinical outcomes. Achieving precise oxygen titration in these infants is particularly challenging, especially in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) with limited staffing resources. Since the 1970s, automated oxygen delivery systems have been developed to assist in the respiratory management of neonates. These systems are integrated into ventilators or oxygen delivery devices and aim to optimize oxygenation automatically. Several clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate their effectiveness. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of automated oxygen delivery systems in preterm infants with respiratory dysfunction who require respiratory support or supplemental oxygen therapy. A comprehensive search of databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, and clinical trial registries, was conducted on January 23, 2023, without restrictions on language or publication date. Reference lists of retrieved articles were also reviewed to identify additional eligible studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and randomized cross-over trials comparing automated oxygen delivery systems with manual oxygen delivery or comparing different automated systems in preterm infants born before 37 weeks of gestation. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes assessed included the percentage of time spent in the desired oxygen saturation (SpO2) range, all-cause in-hospital mortality by 36 weeks' postmenstrual age, severe retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), and neurodevelopmental outcomes at approximately two years of corrected age. Results were expressed using mean difference (MD), standardized mean difference (SMD), and risk ratio (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eighteen studies (27 reports) involving 457 infants were included in the review, with 13 studies (339 infants) contributing data to meta-analyses. Additionally, 13 ongoing studies were identified. The review evaluated three comparisons: (1) automated oxygen delivery versus routine manual oxygen delivery (16 studies), (2) automated oxygen delivery versus enhanced manual oxygen delivery with increased staffing (three studies), and (3) one automated system versus another (two studies). Most studies had a low risk of bias in areas such as blinding of personnel and outcome assessment, incomplete outcome data, and selective outcome reporting. However, many cross-over trials were at high risk of bias due to the lack of separate outcome data for each intervention period. When comparing automated oxygen delivery to routine manual oxygen delivery, automated systems likely increase the percentage of time spent in the desired SpO2 range (MD 13.54%, 95% CI 11.69 to 15.39; moderate-certainty evidence). However, no studies assessed in-hospital mortality in this comparison. Automated oxygen delivery may have little or no effect on the risk of severe ROP (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.94; low-certainty evidence), and no studies evaluated neurodevelopmental outcomes. In the comparison of automated oxygen delivery to enhanced manual oxygen delivery with increased staffing, there may be no clear difference in the percentage of time spent in the desired SpO2 range (MD 7.28%, 95% CI −1.63 to 16.19; low-certainty evidence). No studies in this comparison assessed in-hospital mortality, severe ROP, or neurodevelopmental outcomes. When comparing two automated systems, a revised closed-loop automatic control algorithm (CLACfast), which allows up to 120 automated adjustments per hour, was compared to the original algorithm (CLACslow), which allows up to 20 adjustments per hour. CLACfast may result in little or no difference in the percentage of time spent in the desired SpO2 range compared to CLACslow (MD 3.00%, 95% CI −3.99 to 9.99; low-certainty evidence). No studies assessed in-hospital mortality, severe ROP, or neurodevelopmental outcomes in this comparison. Additionally, a single small study compared the OxyGenie system to the CLiO2 system, but the data were presented as medians and interquartile ranges, making them unsuitable for meta-analysis. In conclusion, automated oxygen delivery systems likely increase the time preterm infants spend in the desired SpO2 range compared to routine manual oxygen delivery. However, it remains unclear whether this improvement translates into significant clinical benefits. The evidence regarding clinical outcomes such as severe ROP is of low certainty, with little or no differences observed between groups. There is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about the effectiveness of automated oxygen delivery compared to enhanced manual oxygen delivery or when comparing different automated systems. Future studies should focus on important shortand long-term clinical outcomes, including mortality, severe ROP, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, intraventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, patent ductus arteriosus, necrotizing enterocolitis, and long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. Parallel-group randomized controlled trials with clear descriptions of staffing levels, particularly in the manual oxygen delivery arm, are needed to ensure reproducibility across different settings. The results of the 13 ongoing studies may provide additional insights and potentially alter the current conclusions and implications for clinical practice and research.
